newsitem.title: UK: IRA bomb suspect faces extradition to Germany.
newsitem.headline: IRA bomb suspect faces extradition to Germany.

text.p: Roisin McAliskey, wanted by German authorities for attempted murder in connection with an IRA mortar attack on a British army base, was remanded in custody for one week in a London court on Wednesday.

Germany has requested the extradition of McAliskey, daughter of former nationalist member of parliament Bernadette McAliskey, nee Devlin. It says she was part of an IRA cell responsible for a mortar attack on a British base in Osnabrueck last June.
McAliskey, 25, spoke only to confirm her name, date of birth and that she understood the charges. She was remanded in custody for one week and will be held at London's Holloway prison.
"She is innocent of the offences of which she is charged," Gareth Pierce, McAliskey's soliticor, told magistrates at Bow Street court.

"They (German authorities) are charging she was a member of a provisional IRA active service unit responsible for the mortar attack on the British barracks," John Pierre Le Tissier, a British police detective, told the court.
Pierce told the court McAliskey was 4-1/2 months pregnant, "represented no threat to the public", and should be released on bail after the next hearing, due to take place on December 4.

"There are complications with this pregnancy," Pierce said. "The doctor who saw her last night (Tuesday) said it was imperative she not go anywhere that does not have specialist obstetrics facilities."
The June 26 attack was one of the IRA's least successful in its fight to end British rule of Northern Ireland.
Only one of three mortar bombs fired at the barracks exploded and that fell several yards (metres) short of its target, a diesel pump for military vehicles. No one was injured.

If extradition is eventually granted, she will be the first person to face charges over the Osnabrueck attack, which was the first in mainland Europe following the end of the IRA ceasefire in February.
Outside court after the hearing, Pierce said she hoped her client would be freed on bail next week.

"She is in poor health and she should certainly not to be going into the conditions provided by the prison service for women prisoners. She will be at physical risk (in prison)," Pierce said. "I hope to have her out as soon as possible."

Since the IRA abandoned its 17-month ceasefire in February, it has set off a series of bombs in Britain. It also staged a car bombing at the British army's headquarters in Northern Ireland in which one soldier was killed.
